articles.title: Zimbabwe minibus carrying church members crashes, killing at least 27
articles.summary: The crash occurred when a truck overtook another vehicle and struck the minibus, police say.
articles.body:
At least 27 people have been killed after a minibus carrying members of a church collided head-on with a haulage truck in central Zimbabwe , police say.

The crash happened at about 18:30 GMT on Friday near Chivhu, about 140km (87 miles) south of the capital, Harare, police spokesperson Paul Nyathi said on Saturday.

The truck was trying to overtake another vehicle when it crashed with the minibus taxi, which was carrying members of a popular African Christian denomination who were travelling for a conference, he said.

State-run broadcaster ZBC News, quoting a provincial government minister, said 23 people died at the scene, while others succumbed to their injuries after being admitted to a local hospital.

Footage shared on social media by ZBC showed the mangled minibus charred to a shell, with the truck on the opposite side of the road.

The crash occurred in a flat, remote stretch of road, with low vegetation lining the roadside and open terrain beyond.

The incident is the latest in a string of deadly crashes on Zimbabwe’s roads, which are riddled with potholes after years of underfunding and neglect.

For everyday transport, many Zimbabweans rely on the privately run minibus taxis, known locally as kombi, but they are often criticised for overloading.

In April, at least 18 people were killed when a minibus burst into flames on a highway in the south, while earlier that month a woman and her five children died when their vehicle collided with a haulage truck on another highway linking Zimbabwe and South Africa.

articles.title: 'Strikes not just near LoC': Ex-Army chief Naravane details how India changed tactics in Op Sindoor
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Former Army chief General M M Naravane on Saturday described Operation Sindoor as \"very necessary action\", stating that it marked a signifi.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Former Army chief General M M Naravane on Saturday described Operation Sindoor as "very necessary action", stating that it marked a significant shift in India's approach towards Pakistan. Naravane said India moved beyond targeting terrorist bases along the border to striking their supporters and infrastructure deep inside Pakistan, signalling a more assertive response to cross-border terrorism.Speaking to reporters in Vadodara after attending an event, Naravane, the 28th Chief of the Army Staff, said India’s earlier responses to terror attacks, including the Uri and Pulwama attacks, had largely focused on terrorist hideouts close to the border.“Operation Sindoor, which took place after the Pahalgam attack, was a very necessary action... Previously, whenever such attacks occurred, like after Uri, and Balakot strikes after Pulwama -- we were mostly targeting terrorist hideouts close to the border,” he said, news agency PTI reported.“But this time, the strikes carried out targeted their supporters and those who provide them backing, wherever they may be -- not just near the Line of Control, but deep inside Pakistan, in Muridke and Bahawalpur, from where they receive this support,” he added.Naravane said the operation sent a message that those supporting terrorism could not escape Indian action regardless of where they were located.“As our defence minister Rajnath Singh had said, 'we will enter their territory and eliminate them', and there will be no protection for them. So, this was a very significant shift in our modus operandi,” he said.Naravane dismisses Pak’s ability to take on IndiaAsked about reports of increased Pakistani activity in the Sir Creek sector and the reported “Operation Ababil”, Naravane said such activities take place but he did not have complete information about the reported operation.“These kinds of activities keep happening. I don't have complete information about this right now since I am retired,” he said.“I would like to say that whatever activity takes place, our forces always keep a close watch on it. There is nothing to panic about, and whatever action needs to be taken, appropriate action will be taken at the right time,” he added.Asked whether Pakistan was capable of taking on India, Naravane replied, “In my opinion, no.”On India-China border talksOn India-China relations, Naravane said the recent meeting between National Security Advisor Ajit Doval and Chinese foreign minister Wang Yi should be viewed against the backdrop of the long-standing boundary dispute between the two countries.“This discussion that took place, the 25th round of Special Representative-level talks between Ajit Doval from our side and Foreign Minister Wang Yi from China, is not happening for the first time,” he said.Naravane said the lack of a clearly demarcated boundary, both on maps and on the ground, was the key issue behind periodic disputes between the two countries.“Exactly where the boundary lies has not been clearly demarcated either on maps or on the ground. It is because of this lack of demarcation that occasional disputes arise between India and China,” he said.On theatre commands, Naravane said the debate over reorganising the armed forces along integrated theatre lines had been underway since the Kargil War.“The discussion on theaterisation first began after the Kargil War. It has already been 25 to 26 years since then. Theaterisation is not a new concept; it is a continuous process and an evolution,” he said.“Considering the way the nature of modern warfare is transforming and decision cycles are becoming progressively shorter, it is essential that we move toward theaterisation as expeditiously as possible,” the former Army chief added.Operation Sindoor was a significant demonstration of India's military and strategic capabilities, combining military and non-military measures to neutralise terrorist threats and deter Pakistani aggression. The multi-dimensional operation reinforced India’s zero-tolerance approach to terrorism while maintaining strategic restraint and securing international support.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Mum of Nottingham attacks victim backs calls to stop killers' early release
articles.summary: Emma Webber has joined more than 30 families in signing an open letter to the government.
articles.body:
More than 30 families have called on the government to stop killers convicted of any form of manslaughter being released early to ease prison overcrowding in England and Wales.

In a letter to Justice Secretary Alex Norris, the families said they felt victims were "being asked to bear the consequences of the prison capacity crisis".

Signatories include Emma Webber, whose son Barnaby was stabbed to death in the Nottingham attacks in 2023 , and whose killer Valdo Calocane was convicted of manslaughter on the basis of diminished responsibility.

Speaking on Radio 4's Today programme, Bridget Phillipson, Minister for Women and Equalities, defended the early release scheme.

She said the government had faced "some really difficult and unpalatable choices" in dealing with prison overcrowding and that they had faced "the wholesale collapse of the criminal justice system".

The scheme aims to ease prison overcrowding in England and Wales.

The families of those affected by homicide have called for those convicted of any form of manslaughter to be excluded.

Those convicted of murder and those serving sentences for rape, serious child sexual abuse and grooming offences are already excluded from the early release scheme.

Calocane fatally stabbed students Barnaby Webber and Grace O'Malley-Kumar, both 19, and school caretaker Ian Coates, 65, on the streets of Nottingham on the morning of 13 June.

He then stole Coates's van and used it to drive into three other people, seriously injuring them.

Calocane admitted three counts of manslaughter and three counts of attempted murder on the basis of diminished responsibility, and was sentenced to an indefinite hospital order in January 2024.

The letter comes after Prime Minister Andy Burnham indicated the government would make changes to the early release scheme to ensure that the killers of PC Andrew Harper , who were convicted of unlawful act manslaughter, are not eligible.

The letter also highlighted concerns that some of the most serious domestic homicides result in convictions of voluntary manslaughter and that it would be "difficult to reconcile with the government's commitment to halve violence against women and girls" if those offenders were released early.

The families said they had "deep concerns about how early release may apply in homicide".

They wrote: "As the government considers excluding unlawful act manslaughter from the scheme, it must follow that all forms of manslaughter are also excluded.

"We have spoken with numerous bereaved families affected by homicide.

"A consistent theme has emerged: many feel that victims are being asked to bear the consequences of the prison capacity crisis through the earlier release of those convicted of the most serious offences.

"Whether intended or not, this is creating a growing sense that justice for victims and public protection are being compromised in order to address pressures elsewhere in the system.

"We therefore urge the government, as it seeks to prevent those responsible for the killing of PC Harper from benefiting from the early release scheme, to ensure that voluntary manslaughter is also brought within the proposed exemption."

John Hunt, whose wife Carol and their daughters Hannah and Louise were killed in their home by Louise's ex-boyfriend Kyle Clifford in 2024. Clifford was convicted of three counts of murder and sentenced to a whole-life order.

Diana Parkes, whose daughter Joanna Simpson was killed by her estranged husband Robert Brown in 2010. Brown was convicted of manslaughter on the basis of diminished responsibility.

John and Penny Clough , the parents of Jane Clough, a nurse who was murdered in 2010.

Josh Rook, whose sister Annabel Rook was murdered by her partner Clifton George in 2025.

Campaigners and victims' organisations have also backed the change.

Frank Mullane, chief executive officer of Advocacy After Fatal Domestic Abuse, said: "The breadth of support for this letter demonstrates the strength of feeling among bereaved families.

"These are not isolated voices. Families from many homicide cases in recent years are united in calling for a clear and consistent approach to homicide and early release."

Jo Early, chief executive officer of Support after Murder and Manslaughter, said: "Bereaved families understand the pressures facing the justice system.

"But they should never feel that justice for victims is being diluted because of those pressures. The most serious offences should be treated consistently and public confidence must be protected."

Currently, 5,000 people are set to be released early, down from 6,000 after some exemptions were announced as part of an urgent review.

Phillipson said: "We have been clear that the most serious offenders will be exempt from that early release programme.

"But the reality of what we are confronting is that, if allowed to go unchecked, we could end up in a position where someone who is arrested for very serious offences, for example offences related to violence against a woman, and we wouldn't have anywhere to send that individual."

A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: "We share the public's anger that these options are even being considered, after we inherited a prison system on the brink of collapse.

"We are fixing this by building 14,000 new prison places, expanding electronic tagging on an unprecedented scale, and investing in probation services at record levels.

"We are also exploring how we can go further, including faster deportation of foreign criminals, better use of the women's estate and reviewing the unjust IPP sentences."

The prime minister has asked the justice secretary to present a plan for further changes of the early release scheme to parliament next month.

Phillipson confirmed that "full details" would be set out before parliament next week.

articles.summary: SHAHJAHANPUR: Two youths who went to meet a woman in a village were allegedly caught by locals, with one of them tied to a tree and beaten. A video of.
articles.body: SHAHJAHANPUR: Two youths who went to meet a woman in a village were allegedly caught by locals, with one of them tied to a tree and beaten. A video of the incident has since gone viral on social media, police said.The incident took place on Friday afternoon in Maholiya Veeran village under Khutar police station, Superintendent of Police Saurabh Dixit said.According to police, the two youths, Radhe and Sonu, had gone to meet a 28-year-old woman. She had been married for about eight years and had recently been in contact with the two men over the phone. The two are her brothers-in-law by relation, police said.The two were talking to the woman when villagers caught them. The FIR states that the villagers suspected the men were trying to take her away.One of the youths was allegedly tied to a tree with a rope and beaten. The video shows him surrounded by villagers, who ask his name and address. He says he is from the Palia area of Lakhimpur Kheri and apologises, saying he made a mistake and would not return.Both youths later fled the village, police said.Khutar police have registered a case against Sonu and Radhe under Section 87 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) for allegedly trying to abduct the woman.Police have also taken note of the viral video. SP Dixit said action would be taken against those who allegedly tied up and assaulted the youths if a complaint is filed.Stay updated with the latest Bareilly news. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: From 'khana bana leti ho' to 'will our lives fit together?' How India's marriage biodata is evolving
articles.summary: India News: Every year, India witnesses a familiar wave - the marriage season. Wedding halls fill up, families revive old contacts, matrimonial apps see a surge, .
articles.body: Every year, India witnesses a familiar wave - the marriage season. Wedding halls fill up, families revive old contacts, matrimonial apps see a surge, and somewhere between the “ladka kya karta hai?” and “ladki ko kya pasand hai?”, the search for a perfect match begins.India records approximately 10 million marriages a year, or roughly 30,000 weddings a day, according to BiodataPlus.in.Amid the rituals, celebrations and matchmaking conversations comes a quieter ritual: the biodata.What looks like a simple one-page profile is, in fact, a snapshot of a changing India, reflecting what families still look for, what young Indians now expect from a partner and how the idea of a “good match” is being rewritten.The old marriage checklistFor years, a marriage biodata followed an almost predictable template: age, height, complexion, caste, salary and family background.For women, descriptions such as “fair”, “homely” and “well-mannered” were not unusual. For men, a stable job, income, property and family status often carried considerable weight.Recalling her experience, 52-year-old Mamata from Uttar Pradesh, told TOI these factors continue to play a major role in rural areas, although expectations have evolved as one moves towards urban India. “During my time, a few family members used to visit the girl’s family and ask questions about her height, age, hobbies and, most importantly, whether she could cook (khana bana leti ho?). The girl’s family wasn’t really allowed to ask questions to the other side. That used to be a very awkward conversation,” she said.But she sees a clear difference in how the next generation approaches marriage.“My daughter has her own perspective and priorities. If parents of my generation were looking for a match for her, we would consider the factors I mentioned above. But those things may not matter to my daughter because she is working and living abroad,” she said.The difference, then, may not simply be about what appears on a biodata. It is also about who gets to decide what matters.What’s changed, and what hasn’tSo, has the marriage biodata itself really changed?Not really.Shalini Singh, founder of matchmaking platform Andwemet, believes the format has remained surprisingly similar, even as expectations around marriage have evolved.“Honestly, the biodata format itself hasn't changed much because what needs to change is the mindset of the people creating them. That kind of change is hard, but it's the only way forward. And the people who are willing to evolve their biodata are the ones finding better matches,” she said.Relationship coach Sidhharrth S Kumaar of NumroVani sees the shift less in the document itself and more in its purpose.According to him, the question is gradually moving from “Is this family socially suitable?” to “Can these two individuals realistically build a life together?”He also points to a change in who controls the process. While parents were once the primary custodians of marriage biodatas, individuals are increasingly taking charge of their own profiles and decisions, sometimes with guidance from relationship or matrimonial coaches and even AI.“Parents use the biodata to reduce social uncertainty, while their children use it to reduce relationship uncertainty,” noted Kumaar.That distinction captures one of the biggest changes in the modern marriage search.Verona Matchmaking, another platform TOI spoke to, points to another broader shift: the changing role of courtship itself. Young Indians increasingly want the opportunity to date, spend time together and genuinely get to know each other before deciding to marry. Which was yes- not a case earlier.But there is an interesting contradiction. As people become better at describing exactly what they want in a partner, there is also a risk of becoming too good at filtering people out.Verona Matchmaking therefore emphasises the importance of keeping an open mind during the process. The objective, it suggests, “should not be to find someone who perfectly matches every item on a checklist, but to find someone worth getting to know.”From 'fitting in' to 'fitting together'For people currently looking for a partner, the shift is increasingly visible in the questions they ask.Rupali Rani, an account manager at The Reppro who is currently looking for a match, told TOI that financial stability is important but no longer enough. “For me, financial stability is only one part of the picture. I want to know how a person thinks, communicates, treats people and looks at life. I would rather have a good conversation with someone and realise that our values align than tick ten boxes on a biodata and then struggle to have a conversation in real life,” she said.For Rani, the change is particularly visible in what women expect from marriage. “It is now less about ‘Will you fit into my family?’ and more about ‘Will our lives fit together?’” she said.“I would rather have an uncomfortable conversation in the beginning than a comfortable misunderstanding that becomes a problem later. My career, my lifestyle and my independence are important to me. Of course, being in a relationship means making adjustments; both people will have to. But adjustment and compromise are not the same thing,” she added.Data cited by the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) also points to broader changes in women’s lives.In India, efforts to delay girls’ marriage have contributed to a decline in marriages before the age of 18, from 47% in 2006 to 23% in 2019-2021. Over the same period, the proportion of girls completing higher secondary education increased from 34% to 48%.The other sideBut women aren't the only ones rewriting the rules of modern matchmaking. Men, too, are pushing back against transactional evaluations in search of genuine emotional alignment.Shivam Sharma, who is currently looking for a match, told TOI that questions about his CTC, job, property, family responsibilities and career plans are common, particularly from the prospective bride’s family.He understands why families ask such questions but believes a man's worth should not be reduced to his income or assets.“Someone may have a very high salary or own properties worth crores, but that doesn't guarantee that he will be a good husband, that he will bring happiness to his partner, or that the relationship will be free from dishonesty or conflicts,” he said.Instead, Sharma believes families should also ask about a man’s ambitions, values, work ethic, financial plans and how he views his responsibilities towards his family.He also sees a change in who gets the final say.“Both families may still be involved, but ultimately, the decision is increasingly being left to the two people who are actually going to spend their lives together. I think that is an important and positive change,” he said.Traditional expectations from women, however, have not disappeared. Sharma said terms such as “good family” and “homely” can still influence matchmaking, but personally, he does not consider appearance-based factors such as height or fairness important.“For me, good nature, mutual understanding, compatibility and family values matter much more than someone's appearance,” he said.He also does not expect his future wife to give up her ambitions, friendships, interests or individuality after marriage.“If she wants to travel, spend time with her friends, watch a movie, go on a long drive or pursue something that makes her happy, I don't think marriage should stop her from doing those things. She should have her own space and freedom, just as I would expect to have mine,” he said.Major decisions, including family planning, should also be discussed and taken jointly, he added.“Marriage should involve adjustments from both sides, not sacrifices expected from only one person,” Sharma said.Biodata vs personFor those who have gone through matchmaking, the importance of a biodata can look different in hindsight. What seems important while searching for a partner may not always matter once two people begin building a life together.Vaibhavi Srivastava, an assistant account manager in corporate communications and PR, and Prakhar Mathur, a software test engineer, are now married. Speaking to TOI, they shared what they looked for in each other's biodatas and how their idea of a “good match” has evolved.Srivastava focused more on the individual than the family. She looked for educational qualifications, career, future plans and a progressive, open-minded partner who would support her ambitions. A relatively small family was also a preference.Mathur initially considered age, but soon focused on personality, education and career goals. He liked that Srivastava had “her own goals and clear ideas regarding her future”.For both, compatibility and mutual support mattered more than ticking boxes. Srivastava now places greater emphasis on family values and communication, while Mathur believes biodatas reveal only so much.“Real priorities will come to the fore during a conversation about your way of communication and your view of life,” he said.Neither considered caste or family status deciding factors. Ultimately, they said, the relationship is between the two people getting married.The old checklist is evolving … slowlyYet the shift towards compatibility does not mean the traditional marriage checklist has disappeared. Caste, complexion, height, income and family background continue to influence partner selection, though their importance varies across families and generations.Sharma believes caste still matters, but the barrier is thinner than it was for his parents' generation. Greater interaction through education, workplaces and social circles, he said, has made young people more open to cross-caste relationships.“I don't think caste has disappeared, but I do think compatibility, understanding and individual choice are becoming more important,” he said, adding that marriage decisions are increasingly about the two people rather than their caste backgrounds.Rani sees a similar transition. Preferences for someone “fair”, “homely” or from a “good family” remain, she said, even as others prioritise stable careers, emotional maturity and shared values.“We are in a transition phase. The old checklist hasn't disappeared; it has simply started sharing space with a new one,” she said.Ankur Gola, a resident of Delhi, who recently got married, told TOI, “my family was on board with whoever I'm considering but there was an orthodox condition that person should not be of lower cast or muslim; which was difficult for me to accept as they never taught me to discriminate against people... I decided to break the cycle.”New words, old biases Sidhharrth Kumaar takes the argument a step further. He believes traditional factors have not necessarily disappeared, they have sometimes simply been given newer names.Caste, he said, may be described as “cultural compatibility” or “similar traditions”. Complexion and appearance may become “presentable”, “well-groomed” or “fitness-conscious”, while family status may appear as “similar upbringing”, “compatible lifestyle” or “well-settled family”.Even the phrase “our vibes did not match”, he said, can sometimes become a convenient umbrella for discomfort related to appearance, accent, class, caste-coded habits or family culture without explicitly naming the criterion.“These expressions are not inherently discriminatory, but they can camouflage older preferences. The language of matchmaking has modernised faster than the underlying selection criteria,” he said.The transition, therefore, is not a clean break from the past.The vocabulary of matchmaking may be changing, but some of the old filters continue to quietly shape who gets considered a “good match”.The big pictureThe traditional one-page marriage biodata is no longer confined to a printed sheet passed between relatives, family friends or neighbours.Increasingly, matchmaking has moved online, with profiles becoming searchable, editable and instantly shareable.That has changed the reach of the biodata.What once travelled through a limited family or community network can now be shared far beyond it, sometimes with hundreds or thousands of potential matches.Yet technology has not necessarily erased tradition.Instead, the old checklist has found a new home online.A profile can still ask about caste, family, profession and income, even as it increasingly includes interests, lifestyle, career aspirations and expectations from a partner.The format has become digital. The conversation around it is becoming more personal.And perhaps that is the real evolution of the Indian marriage biodata.It is no longer only asking, “Is this person suitable for our family?”Increasingly, the question is becoming:“Can these two people build a life that works for both of them?”The biodata may still fit on one page. But the definition of a “good match” is getting much bigger.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: UNRWA’s first and last vocational college in East Jerusalem is under threat
articles.summary: Israel threatens the Qalandiya Training Centre, one of Jerusalem’s oldest still-operational educational institutions.
articles.body:
Qalandiya, West Bank – By midday Friday, Israeli troops had withdrawn from the Qalandiya Training Centre in occupied East Jerusalem, but overhead, an Israeli drone still hovered in the sky, likely filming and monitoring any activity below.

For now, occupied East Jerusalem’s last remaining vocational training centre remains off-limits to Palestinians. Meanwhile, Israeli troops are threatening to storm at any time.

Looking through the UNRWA centre’s main gate, the aftermath of a previous Israeli raid was evident: Shattered glass, the remnants of metal and charred ground.

Other videos Al Jazeera obtained from the training facility show classrooms ransacked, doors smashed and workshops abandoned.

UNRWA confirmed damage to the facility when Israeli troops were present and said it had received reports of “individuals entering the premises and attempting to steal some of its contents”.

Registration for the new school year was open until September 1, and classes were to begin soon. UNRWA says it hopes to reopen the facility at the earliest possible opportunity.

But on Tuesday, Israeli military and police personnel raided the centre and surrounding areas, expelling about 40 staff members.

The Qalandiya Training Centre has already been raided six times this year, UNRWA said.

But this time it was different, with Israel’s National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir accompanying the police during the incursion.

“Here sat the director of UNRWA, and now I sit in his place,” he said.

The Israeli Ministry of Foreign Affairs also said on social media that the land will be handed to the Jerusalem municipality and turned into an educational complex.

But that’s exactly what the centre currently is – an educational facility giving Palestinian refugees the chance to study and join the workforce.

Each year, about 340 Palestinian refugees from across the occupied West Bank graduate from the training centre.

After they complete a two-year programme, they can obtain vocational diplomas in 16 specialisations, including carpentry, telecommunications, and interior design.

For many, this is a chance to get the skills needed to join the workforce, build a life and a career. The United Nations says 90% of the graduates from the facility find a job, which is a remarkable achievement given that nearly one in three Palestinians in the occupied West Bank are out of work.

The centre has been running for more than seven decades, and one of its graduates is 73-year-old Youssef Abu Latifeh, who lives as a refugee in the Qalandiya refugee camp.

At his home, he shows us his architectural drawing diploma. Printed in 1974, some of the ink has faded, but UNRWA’s blue stamp and Youssef’s grades are still visible.

He was 20 years old when he graduated from the centre. It helped him secure a job in a Greek company in Libya, before returning to his refugee camp in the occupied West Bank.

“If it wasn’t for the centre, I wouldn’t have finished my studies. My father worked at the UN, and his simple salary was barely able to sustain our big family, let alone send me to a university. So, I owe the centre a lot,” Youssef told Al Jazeera.

He had heard the news about the centre being threatened with closure, but didn’t think it would actually happen.

“It’s too painful to see how many people will be deprived of this crucial opportunity,” he told Al Jazeera.

The centre was established in 1952 on an eight-hectare (20-acre) plot of land, rented to UNRWA by the Jordanian government, which at the time administered the West Bank and East Jerusalem, before Israel’s occupation of the territory.

While Israeli authorities claim the land belongs to the Jewish National Fund, and has been handed to the Jerusalem Municipality, UNRWA says the premises are protected by the privileges and immunities of the UN under international law.

UNRWA also stressed that the centre is in occupied East Jerusalem and is part of occupied Palestinian territory, so Israel has no sovereign jurisdiction over the land.

In 1980, Israel illegally declared the annexation of occupied East Jerusalem – but it had been working on this since its 1967 occupation of the Palestinian territory.

Palestinians, like Youssef, say the war on UNRWA isn’t really about the land or buildings, but another attempt to erase what the agency represents: Palestinian refugees’ plight and their right of return.

Israel’s campaign against the UN agency for Palestinian refugees has escalated in recent years. In 2024, Israel’s Knesset passed several anti-UNRWA laws.

Israeli authorities also stopped issuing visas or permits to UNRWA’s international staff since the end of January 2025.

In May 2025, Israeli authorities forcibly closed six UNRWA schools in occupied East Jerusalem, including the schools in Shu’fat Camp, affecting approximately 800 children.

In January 2026, Israeli authorities took over the UNRWA headquarters in occupied East Jerusalem and demolished mobile offices there.

UNRWA has already been suffering a deep financial crisis. This has been made worse by Israel’s freezing of the agency’s funds after alleging it had ties with Hamas, despite providing no adequate proof to back its claims. Still, the damage has been done.

articles.title: A Mexican entrepreneur turned discarded plastic into low-cost homes for families in poverty; each 430-460 sq ft house used 2 tonnes of waste, took 7 days to build and cost families about $280
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Plastic production has increased exponentially over the last few decades. A 2017 study published in Science Advances estimated that 8.3 billion tons o.
articles.body: Plastic production has increased exponentially over the last few decades. A 2017 study published in Science Advances estimated that 8.3 billion tons of plastic have been produced globally since large-scale production began. Only a tiny fraction has been recycled, with huge amounts accumulating in landfills, ecosystems and waterways. Mexico has a big plastic problem of its own. The country consumes hundreds of thousands of tons of PET every year and is one of the largest consumers of bottled water and soft drinks in the world. Mexico has made progress in recycling, too. In the last 15 years, PET collection and recycling rates have risen substantially, proving how awareness can be translated into concrete action. An example of this approach is González’s EcoDom project. According to a news report by Eleconomista website, González was raised in the mountains of Puebla, a region rife with poverty and little access to proper housing. His experiences helped shape his interest in finding solutions that can solve both housing needs and plastic pollution. In 2013 he created the model which would be the basis of EcoDom. The company doesn’t see plastic as waste, but as a potential construction resource. Its raw materials are PET, as well as high-density polyethylene, polypropylene and ABS plastics found in products ranging from containers and buckets to toys and bags. EcoDom collects plastic from small businesses, independent collectors and organized collection campaigns. The material is sorted, processed and ground into flakes, then placed into molds, heated and pressed into construction components.Recycling for building materialsThe report highlights that they produce materials for structural walls, slabs, mezzanines and thermal roofing systems. González says each wall requires about six kilograms of processed plastic. The system provides an alternative to traditional masonry, while reducing the amount of plastic that enters the environment. The company’s model combines commercial activity with a social mission. It earns revenue by selling construction materials, offering construction services and building housing for people who cannot afford it. Some of the revenues go toward social programs, like helping to subsidize homes for families that otherwise would struggle to pay for them.Homes affordable for low-income familiesEcoDom’s subsidized housing model is specifically designed to ensure affordability for low-income households. The company's figures state that complete homes of about 42 square meters can be provided for roughly 5,000 Mexican pesos, or about $280. Single-bedroom buildings and other smaller units can be much cheaper. Families can also contribute labor, making the model more accessible for those with limited cash. The homes are designed to be constructed far quicker than traditional buildings. A house built with the system is said to be finished in a week, and the company says its materials can be more resistant to some loads than traditional masonry.A soial mission beyond buildingThe work of EcoDom has gone beyond the sale of houses. The company has also started giving houses to families in need. It has already sold two homes, given away five homes and three bedrooms and is seeking more partnerships to provide more housing. One possible collaboration is with the Universidad Cuauhtémoc de Puebla.The project has also attracted attention internationally. González said that companies and organizations from India, Canada, France, Brazil, South Africa, Guatemala and the Dominican Republic have shown interest in the technology.Expanding on the ideaThe investment to develop the business is more than eight million Mexican pesos. Now González is looking at franchising EcoDom and expanding the concept to communities beyond Puebla. The firm is also gearing up for a project to build 250 houses in Puebla, with plans to provide materials and training for at least part of the development. The premise of EcoDom is simple: waste does not necessarily have to stay waste. González’s model aims to tackle two enduring problems at once – plastic pollution and the lack of good quality, affordable housing – through the combination of recycling and affordable construction. If scaled up successfully, such approaches could show how discarded materials can be used in practical solutions for communities, while giving plastic waste a second life.Images Courtesy: Unreasonable Group and EcoDomCatch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Mutinous soldiers attack airport, presidency in Niger capital
articles.summary: Mutinous soldiers in Niger attacked the airport and the presidency in the capital, Niamey, ​early on Saturday, triggering hours of sustained gunfire and explosions and briefly knocking state television and radio off air.
articles.body: Mutinous soldiers in Niger attacked the airport and the presidency in the capital, Niamey, ​early on Saturday, triggering hours of sustained gunfire and explosions and briefly knocking state television and radio off air. By ‌late morning, Niger’s defense ministry said the armed forces were progressively retaking control of sites targeted in the overnight attack, but security sources said mutineers were still present at the airport and the overall situation remained unclear. The attack marked the latest threat to the rule of Abdourahamane Tiani, who seized power in a 2023 ​coup. Tiani had pledged to improve security in the Sahel nation, a major uranium producer, but jihadist attacks have persisted. State ​television, after resuming broadcasts, aired a message saying mutinous soldiers from a base in Niamey had opened fire ⁠on “sensitive sites” in the city. Security forces had reacted quickly and “contained this disturbance”, it said. A Reuters witness reported gunfire at the airport and heavy explosions in the pre-dawn hours. As of 0900 GMT, the presidential palace appeared to have been secured by loyalist troops but the area around the airport was still contested, two security sources and a diplomat said. Two ​sources said that loyalist troops had been dispatched to retake control of the airport, either through negotiations or by force. The assault also involved ​soldiers from the localities of Ouallam, Tera and Dosso in the southwest, according to a Niger security source and Yvan Guichaoua, senior researcher at the ‌Bonn International ⁠Centre for Conflict Studies. Troops in this area have sustained heavy casualties in battles with the regional Islamic State affiliate, and analysts and security sources say frustration with the government is mounting within frontline units. It was not clear how many troops allied with the mutineers had entered Niamey or where they had deployed. Earlier this year, affiliates of al Qaeda and ​Islamic State both carried out attacks on the civilian airport and military airbase, contributing to initial suspicion that militants could have been behind the ​assault on the capital. Niger, a mineral-rich West African nation with significant uranium, oil and gold resources, has been ruled ​by military officers since the July ​2023 coup that ousted President ⁠Mohamed Bazoum. Like its neighbors Burkina Faso and Mali, it has failed to turn the tide in its battle against Islamist insurgencies linked to al Qaeda and Islamic State despite pledges by military rulers to improve security. West ​Africa’s al Qaeda affiliate claimed responsibility for an attack on the airport in Niamey in June, five ​months after Islamic ⁠State Sahel Province targeted the same site. Since seizing power, Tiani’s government has shifted away from Western partners, deepened ties with Russia and broken with the regional ECOWAS bloc, joining Mali and Burkina Faso to form the breakaway AES bloc. The unrest comes as authorities tighten control over its uranium sector, having seized ⁠assets from ​France’s Orano. Niger had been a key supplier of nuclear fuel to Europe, accounting ​for about 15% of Orano’s uranium supply at full capacity. Last week, the government reallocated former Orano and GoviEx uranium permits to state-backed companies, according to a decree.

articles.title: As Lindsay Clancy jury deliberates, US mother found not guilty in deaths of 2 children
articles.summary: US News: A Bronx judge has found a mother of two not guilty by reason of insanity in the 2022 deaths of her young children, ruling that she was not criminally .
articles.body: A Bronx judge has found a mother of two not guilty by reason of insanity in the 2022 deaths of her young children, ruling that she was not criminally responsible because of severe mental illness. The case has drawn fresh attention as a Massachusetts jury deliberates the fate of Lindsay Clancy, who is accused of killing her three children amid claims that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis.Dimone Fleming, 26, was found not responsible by mental disease or defect for the deaths of her 3-year-old son Daishawn Fleming and 11-month-old Octavius Canada at a family shelter in the Bronx.Mental health experts for both the prosecution and defence concluded that Fleming was experiencing psychosis at the time of the killings.A prosecution psychiatrist said Fleming was “grossly psychotic and out of touch with reality”, experiencing hallucinations and believing that a spirit had invaded her body. Defence experts said she believed her actions were necessary to protect or “cleanse” her children.Fleming had previously spent about two months receiving treatment at a Queens hospital, where she was diagnosed with major depressive disorder and prescribed psychiatric medication.However, court records showed she did not consistently take the medication and was using marijuana daily, which reportedly worsened her symptoms.The children were found with multiple stab wounds in a bathtub after a shelter employee called 911 on November 26, 2022, reporting water and smoke coming from Fleming’s apartment.Police initially took Fleming to a hospital for evaluation after finding her behaving irrationally. The children’s bodies were discovered later after their father, Columbus Canada, went to the apartment.Fleming, who was then 22, had been charged with first-degree murder. Prosecutors told the court that pursuing a double-murder trial would not serve justice, while stressing the importance of public discussion around such cases.Fleming will remain in custody for now and undergo another psychiatric evaluation to determine whether she poses a threat to others. She is due back in court on September 18, and could remain in a psychiatric hospital for months or years.Canada, Octavius's father, attended Monday’s hearing and said he forgives Fleming. He described her as a “good person” and a loving mother.Lindsay Clancy caseThe Bronx ruling comes as jurors in Massachusetts deliberate in the closely watched case of Lindsay Clancy, who is accused of killing her three children — 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan — at their Duxbury home in January 2023.Clancy’s defence has argued that she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis and bipolar disorder when she strangled the children before attempting suicide.Prosecutors, however, have argued that the killings were intentional and planned. After five weeks of testimony, the jury began deliberations on August 27.The two cases have drawn comparisons over the role of postpartum psychosis in mothers accused of killing their children. Experts say postpartum psychosis is rare but can involve hallucinations, delusions and a severe break from reality, with symptoms emerging after childbirth.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Korea divided: A sister’s long wait and a defector’s bid to save his mother
articles.summary: An elderly South Korean waits to see a brother in the North one last time, while a North Korean defector risks it all.
articles.body:
This feature is part of a series examining how artificial borders reshape daily life, divide families and force loved ones to navigate the human cost of political geography.

Kang Myung Sook was 63 the last time she saw her brother in North Korea. She is 87 now and lives in an elderly care facility in rural South Korea, about 32 kilometres (20 miles) from the border with the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea.

For two days in 2002, the siblings sat across from each other in a hotel banquet hall in a North Korean resort town, surrounded by hundreds of other families doing the same thing: trying to compress 50 years of life, thoughts and memories into a handful of hours, with government minders standing close enough to hear every word.

Then, the buses came to take the families home, half to North Korea, half to South Korea.

“My brother called out from the window of the moving bus, telling me to take care of myself,” Kang said. “We were all crying — it was chaotic. And then we never saw each other again.”

She is one of roughly 34,000 living South Koreans officially registered with the government as separated from family members in North Korea by the Korean War — a fraction of the 134,500 who have registered since the government began keeping records in 1988. More than 100,000 others have since died.

But the registry only counts those who applied, mostly for a shot at the now-suspended reunion programme. It says nothing about the far larger, uncounted number of Koreans — descendants, distant relatives, childhood friends, North Korean escapees — who still carry some connection to someone on the other side of the border.

This is a story about two of them: a woman who has been waiting nearly 75 years for the war between North and South to end properly, and a young man who managed to get back across the line separating both Koreas — twice — to bring the last of his family out.

articles.title: Birmingham woman detained in Egypt over 'sister's activist videos'
articles.summary: There has been no contact with Eman el-Shazly since she was detained, her husband says.
articles.body:
A mother-of-four from Birmingham has been detained by the Egyptian authorities, with her husband and lawyer claiming it is due to her sister's online activism.

Eman el-Shazly, 45, from Handsworth Wood, was taken from her mother's house in Cairo in the early hours of Monday 17 August. Her husband, Zeesharn Moustapha, said this was 24 hours after Egyptian security forces "ram-raided" the property and told her: "You need to tell your sister to stop".

Three of el-Shazly's other siblings have also been detained, with her two brothers already being held when she was taken, and one of her sisters detained soon after.

The BBC has contacted the Egyptian consulate in London but has not had a response.

Moustapha said: "The family's a bit traumatised. [The children] are heartbroken.

"We really need the UK government to get their fingers out as quickly as possible."

A spokesperson for the Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) said: "We are supporting the family of a British national detained in Egypt, and are in contact with the authorities."

Moustapha told the BBC that his wife had travelled to Egypt to look after her elderly, sick mother, who had been undertaking 18-hour round-trips to take food to el-Shazly's two brothers in detention.

He claimed this was because Egyptian detention centres did not feed the people held there.

"There's 30 people in a cell and they all sleep on a concrete floor. Each day one inmate's family brings food for all people," Moustapha said.

"If that family cannot afford it, they don't eat. Imagine the worst scenario, and it's even worse."

He said his wife had travelled to Egypt to help her mother with "all the headache" relating to this.

However, in the early hours of Sunday 16 August, Moustapha said Egyptian security forces "ram-raided" the house in Cairo, and told el-Shazly to stop her sister from criticising the Egyptian government in her YouTube videos.

"They went into the property and smashed the place up, even bending forks and knives," he said.

Around 24 hours later, he said el-Shazly called him, screaming "they're coming to get me".

Since then, the mother-of-four has been detained in the 10th Ramadan Rehabilitation Centre, which Egyptian authorities have confirmed to the FCDO.

Her lawyer, Arfan Rashid of Rashid Law, told the BBC: "These are trumped up charges and an attempt by Egyptian authorities to silence a political activist in the UK – her sister.

"In my opinion, there is ample and compelling evidence this is just punishment by proxy."

He added that her detention formed part of a "longstanding and documented pattern of pressure" upon her sister.

Her sister told the BBC that she was sorry that her family had been detained. She said this was a tactic used by the Egyptian government to silence critics. But she would not stop posting her videos because she felt it was her duty to make a stand.

In the UK government's country policy and information note on Egypt from March 2026, it references reports surrounding the targeting of the relatives of activists.

Rashid added that if el-Shazly had been wanted by Egyptian authorities, she would have been detained when she entered the country.

"There is a history of authorities targeting these families who have people in their family who are activists," he said.

Furthermore, el-Shazly's has the same case file number as her two brothers, Hassan and Eid, who Rashid says face "substantially identical allegations".

The brothers were initially arrested in 2020 and spent nearly three years in pre-trial detention before being released.

However, they were subsequently arrested again at their home on 19 May and their detention has repeatedly been renewed.

Moustapha said that no one had broken any laws and that his wife's detention was "just punishment for her sister making videos."

"Her family has historically been tortured," he added, alleging that her cousin had been electrocuted while in detention for four days and had been unable to speak since.

There has been no contact with el-Shazly since she has been detained.

Moustapha said he was concerned by what he described as the UK government's "lacklustre at best" involvement, and in particular that no wellness check had yet taken place.

He added that he had to inform the FCDO where his wife was being held.

The FCDO did not comment on these allegations when asked by the BBC.

Moustapha said the majority of support he had received was from Perry Barr MP Ayoub Khan and from Rashid Law.

He now hopes the case will be escalated to Alistair Burt, the UK's first ever envoy for complex consular cases.

While he and his family wait for any news on el-Shazly and her three siblings, 12 children wait for news about their parents.

articles.title: Tens of thousands mourn King Harald V in Oslo as Norway enters a new royal era
articles.summary: Tens of thousands of mourners paid their respects to Norway’s King Harald V on Saturday, placing flowers and condolence cards outside the royal palace in Oslo a day after the monarch died at 89.
articles.body: OSLO, Norway — Tens of thousands of mourners paid their respects to Norway’s King Harald V on Saturday, placing flowers and condolence cards outside the royal palace in Oslo a day after the monarch died at 89. A sea of colorful flowers covered Slottsplassen, the square in front of the palace, as a steady stream of Norwegians filed past. A palace gardener removed some bouquets on the south side of the palace to keep pathways clear, Norwegian broadcaster NRK reported. Palace workers also collected cards soaked after a nightly downpour and dried them to preserve the mourners’ messages for posterity, NRK reported. Across the country, churches and city halls opened specially on Saturday so people could light candles, write down their thoughts about the deceased king in condolence books. The coffin arrived at the royal palace Friday evening from the National Hospital in Oslo where Harald died. “It’s special, intimate, and lovely. I’m placing my right hand on my chest in gratitude to him and the royal family,” Roni Ervik, 46, told NRK as he paid his respects. He said he was also paying tribute to the late king on behalf of his family, who are from western Norway. Harald V died Friday morning and his 53-year-old son, Crown Prince Haakon, became King Haakon VIII. Haakon adopted the motto “All for Norway,” which dates back to his great-grandfather. His wife became Queen Mette-Marit, while his oldest child, Ingrid Alexandra, became crown princess and heir to the throne. Haakon is well acquainted with his royal obligations. As his father aged and his health declined in recent years, he stepped in as the country’s regent on several occasions. Later Saturday, a choir was expected to sing in the Royal Palace Square. The new king was also scheduled to hold audiences with the speaker of Norway’s parliament, the chief justice of the Supreme Court and the presiding bishop of the Lutheran Church of Norway, with Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra also expected to attend, NRK reported. Haakon is expected to address the people of Norway in his first speech as king either later Saturday or in the coming days. His tasks in the near future will include shoring up support for the monarchy following controversies over his wife’s past contacts with deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and his stepson’s rape conviction. A date for the funeral has not been set, but the country is officially in a state of mourning and some people decided to postpone celebrations such as weddings and baptisms until after the mourning period has passed, NRK reported. Norway’s monarchy has old roots, tracing its origins to King Harald Fairhair in the ninth century. When Norway regained its independence from Sweden in 1905, three-quarters of voters in a national plebiscite approved restoring the monarchy. Today, the role is largely symbolic as power lies with an elected parliament, but the country’s royal family retains celebrity and a role in promoting the wealthy nation around the world.

articles.title: Tech investor mocks Vance’s call to hire Americans as 'DEI', gets blasted by Trump officials in H-1B firestorm
articles.summary: Y Combinator investor Ankit Gupta mocked JD Vance's call to prioritize hiring Americans over H-1B visas, sparking backlash from the Trump administration.
articles.body: Ankit Gupta, a general partner at the influential Silicon Valley startup accelerator Y Combinator, drew criticism from Trump administration officials after mocking Vice President JD Vance’s call to prioritize American workers over hiring cheaper foreign labor. The controversy began after the Trump administration proposed a $103,265 fee for many new H-1B visa petitions. As it stands, the H-1B visa program allows U.S. companies to hire foreign workers for specialty occupations and is overwhelmingly used by the tech industry. However, it has long been controversial among some conservatives, who say it is abused by tech companies to bring in cheap labor to replace American workers, many of them from India. The proposed fee would make it costlier for American tech companies to rely on such labor and could give them an incentive to hire Americans instead, something Vance has emphasized repeatedly, such as when he recently declared, "If an American corporation needs workers, it should hire and train Americans." Y Combinator general partner Ankit Gupta, who has since restricted his X posts from public access, mocked Vance, saying in purported screenshots, "In a win for the woke left DEI is back." VANCE WARNS THERE WILL BE A 'SOCIALIST PRESIDENT IN THIS COUNTRY' IF GOP DOESN'T FIX ECONOMY FOR YOUNG PEOPLE Gupta's comments comparing prioritizing American workers over foreign labor to DEI sparked a wave of criticism from several Trump administration officials and renewed a broader debate over H-1B visas, Silicon Valley hiring practices, and whether American workers—particularly younger and entry-level tech workers—are being disadvantaged by companies’ reliance on foreign-worker visa programs. Labor Department Inspector General Anthony D’Esposito replied, "Ankit Gupta thinks hiring Americans first—in America—is ‘DEI.’ No, Ankit. It’s called putting your own citizens first. American companies. American jobs. American workers first. If that offends you, the problem isn’t America. It’s your sense of entitlement." FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson criticized Gupta’s rhetoric as part of a larger phenomenon of contempt for American workers. "I’m deeply uncomfortable with wealthy investors attacking American workers like this. I’m afraid it’s increasingly obvious to many people that individuals such as this guy do not have the best interests of America and her citizens in mind," he said. "The purpose of the American economy is to promote the general welfare of American workers, not provide jobs for the rest of the world." In response to Ferguson's post, Y Combinator President and CEO Garry Tan wrote, "YC supports hiring and funding Americans." Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights Harmeet Dhillon also weighed in, sharing a lengthy post criticizing what she described as abuses of the H-1B program and other foreign-worker programs. "Our federal (and most state) employment laws mandate a level playing field for American workers vis-à-vis foreigners — yet many American tech (and other) companies prefer to hire cheaper/exploitable foreign workers to do routine jobs Americans could do, and they do this by failing to post jobs on their normal hiring channels (PERM violations), letting foreign-born hiring managers pipeline cheap foreign labor from body-shop mills over American workers (H1-B abuses), lie about their eligibility for no-cap H1-B hiring, abuse other visa categories such as J-1 visas (we see you, universities!), abuse OPT hiring to get cheap, exploitable foreign labor, and sometimes — getting super arrogant, gaslight laid-off and sidelined Americans while doing any of the above," she wrote. CEO UNDER FIRE FOR MASS LAYOFFS AMID FOREIGN WORKER HIRING SPREE NOW APPOINTED TO FED'S TASK FORCE ON JOBS Other commentators, ranging from policy think tanks to former Trump officials, spoke to Fox News Digital about the controversy. John Miano, an attorney with the Federation for American Immigration Reform (FAIR), said the debate speaks to fundamental questions about the role of the United States and its immigration system. "The center of this dispute is over what America is. I, and I think most Americans, believe America as a nation state; a commonwealth for the improvement of its citizens. Mr. Gupta clearly views America as an [economic] zone. The graves at Arlington and cemeteries around the world are not the product of Americans fighting and dying to save an economic zone. I would not want to share a foxhole with Mr. Gupta," he told Fox News Digital. He added, "There is no such thing as the [Libertarian] ideal of economics without borders. I would wager that Mr. Gupta opposes open borders regarding intellectual property. The H-1B program is designed to replace Americans with cheap foreign workers. The U.S. Congress is apparently the only national legislature that has voted to make it explicitly legal to replace citizens with foreign workers, as it has done with H-1B. The H-1B wage system is designed to allow employers to pay H-1B nonimmigrants extremely low wages. The biggest problem with H-1B is that it works exactly as Congress designed it to work." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Former Trump Appointee and Senior Advisor to the U.S. Senate, Mary Marslender, now a Republican consultant, explained how tech companies specifically find loopholes in the rules to avoid hiring Americans, particularly those trying to enter the job market. "The uncomfortable reality is that many large American corporations prefer cheaper foreign labor because it gives them greater control over mid- to entry-level positions, all while telling Washington that qualified American workers can't be found. Immigration lawyers have been caught on video admitting their goal is to avoid hiring qualified Americans," she said. "Some have even confessed to placing job ads in obscure newspapers where Americans are unlikely to look, and then, if a qualified American applies, interviewing them specifically to find a legal basis to disqualify them. Prioritizing cheap foreign labor over American workers denies Americans jobs, particularly young people who need the firsthand job experience to launch their careers. American jobs should go to Americans first." Theo Wold, a former acting assistant attorney general and former White House deputy assistant to the president for domestic policy under Trump, argued that part of what makes America great historically is its amazing pool of native talent. "Jack St. Clair Kilby and Robert Noyce invented the microchip. They also both grew up in America's heartland. From airplanes and the television to nuclear submarines and the internet, American genius invented the modern world. But today's Silicon Valley elites would rather replace the next Robert Noyce with a foreign national on an H-1B visa than invest in American talent. America has a unique convergence of brainpower and risk tolerance. And our young people took the challenge and are excelling in STEM," he said. "America now graduates enough American STEM students to fill every opening in America’s tech and tech-related industries. We should be encouraging our young talent to build anew, rather than replace them with cheap labor widgets from Guangdong and Andhra Pradesh." Fox News Digital reached out to Y Combinator for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

articles.title: Tornado and hail hits northern Italian city, injuring dozens of people
articles.summary: Dozens of people were injured after a tornado and hail hit the northern Italian city of Cremona, causing widespread damage.
articles.body: Dozens of people were injured after a tornado and hail hit the northern Italian city of Cremona, causing widespread damage. Like much of Europe, Italy has faced a relentless period of extreme weather, with the country sweltering under its fifth heatwave of the summer. Ten churches, including the city’s main cathedral, were damaged, according to Italy’s fire brigade, which responded to more than 500 emergency calls within hours. A spire fell from one of the cathedral’s towers, altering the city’s most famous landmark. Many of the historic churches suffered extensive damage to their windows and skylights. Twelve families were evacuated after their homes were damaged either by flying debris or the loss of roofs. Hundreds of trees fell, and many homes suffered roof damage, and 10,000 cars were damaged due to a hailstorm and falling trees after the tornado passed, the fire brigade said. Several barns were also heavily damaged, and many low-lying roads were flooded. The cost of the damage is expected to reach millions of euros, according to the city government. The city of Cremona, known for its Stradivari instrument-making, was holding a local festival when the storm hit, causing extensive damage to the pavilions and multiple injuries, according to Francesca Co, director of the city’s emergency services. “Most (of the injured) have been discharged, one remains under observation, while four trauma patients require hospitalization,” she said. “We found ourselves managing the arrival of over forty people almost simultaneously, and the emergency system responded promptly.” Tornados are relatively rare in Italy, and there were no watches or warnings for the possibility of such a weather event were issued, according to Italy’s civil protection agency. On Saturday, the fire brigade and civil defense carried out inspections of buildings. Roads were closed, and the forestry department was carrying out inspections on the so-called “violin forests” from which the city’s famous instruments are made.

articles.title: Operation Economic Outcast needs an off-ramp, not just a noose
articles.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced Operation Economic Outcast on Aug. 24, a massive expansion of sanctions aimed at severing Iran’s ties to the global economy by targeting the infrastructure used for evasion.
articles.body:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent did not undersell it. Announcing Operation Economic Outcast on Aug. 24, he framed it as an “economic D‑Day,” a deliberate invocation of allied resolve to justify what he described as an unprecedented effort to sever Iran’s remaining ties to the global economy. The language is dramatic. The harder question is whether the policy can deliver what the rhetoric promises.

Strip away the framing and the announcement marks a real escalation in scope, even if not in kind. Treasury issued five sectoral sanctions determinations at once — digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping — rather than continuing the piecemeal approach of targeting individual transactions.

Under Executive Order 13902, these determinations give the Office of Foreign Assets Control a basis to designate foreign persons operating in, or providing services or support to, those sectors, wherever they are located.

According to Treasury’s release, the Office of Foreign Assets Control also designated nearly 60 entities, individuals and vessels tied to nuclear and missile procurement, cyber operations linked to Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence and Security, and sprawling shadow‑fleet shipping networks stretching from Hong Kong to Switzerland.

The Office of Foreign Assets Control also suspended several general licenses, including one covering academic exchanges and certain educational services, as well as licenses authorizing specified remittance activity. New guidance tied sanctions risk to shipping decisions around the Strait of Hormuz.

Washington has mounted broad Iran sanctions campaigns before. What distinguishes this one is its attempt to treat the infrastructure of evasion — brokers, exchange houses, logistics firms, and front companies — as targets in their own right. Bessent’s language captures the intent: a “ zero‑leakage” system, backed by deadlines the administration says it has communicated privately to foreign governments, and the threat that any institution facilitating Iran‑linked money laundering will be cut off from the U.S. dollar system.

For all its breadth, the Aug. 24 action stopped short of one of its most consequential possible moves: sanctioning major Chinese financial institutions. China remains Iran’s largest oil buyer and one of Tehran’s most important commercial outlets.

The new designations touch Chinese and Hong Kong‑based procurement and shipping networks, but not the country’s major banks — a step Washington has so far avoided, as a Donald Trump‑Xi Jinping meeting is planned in Washington for Sept. 24 and the administration seeks to preserve a fragile trade truce with Beijing.

Asked whether the United States might go easy on China to preserve that relationship, Bessent said that “ no one is above the reach of U.S. sanctions ” — without specifying when or how that threat would be enforced.

That makes the announcement both an enforcement action and an ultimatum. If Washington ultimately declines to confront those institutions, Iran may retain a crucial outlet regardless of how many secondary intermediaries are sanctioned. If it does act, it risks folding an already complex Iran policy into a far larger U.S.-China confrontation.

The campaign’s credibility will turn less on the number of names added to the sanctions list this week than on whether Washington is prepared to impose costs on the actors whose cooperation has proven hardest to obtain.

The campaign rests on a familiar coercive diplomacy assumption: that enough economic pressure can force a change in behavior. History suggests a more complicated reality. Regimes facing existential pressure do not reliably negotiate; they often adapt.

The relevant question is not whether sanctions can cause pain — they clearly can — but whether the target believes compliance will produce durable relief, and whether the demands are limited enough to accept without threatening the regime’s survival.

Iran has spent decades refining tools for this scenario: discounted oil sales, front companies, barter, informal finance, and cryptocurrency. Its political economy gives the regime strong incentives to protect hard currency for security institutions first, pushing the adjustment cost onto ordinary households, producing a poorer, more securitized Iran rather than a more compliant one.

This has direct regional implications. Tehran’s influence in Iraq and Lebanon is sustained partly through financial and logistical networks this campaign aims to disrupt. Weakening those networks may reduce Iran’s capacity to project power through allied militias, but financial stress can also make those actors less predictable, especially where proxies retain autonomy from Tehran.

The humanitarian dimension is easy to overlook. Suspending licenses covering certain remittances and cultural or academic transactions may close channels that matter little to the regime’s revenue but matter a great deal to ordinary Iranians.

None of this means the campaign is destined to fail. It means the outcome depends on choices Washington has not yet made public.

Economic isolation is a tool, not a strategy. A negotiated settlement requires specifying what Tehran must do, what relief is available in return, and how compliance would be verified, because “reintegration” without those terms reads less like an offer than a demand for surrender.

Credible assurances that compliance would not simply trigger new demands.

If the goal is outright capitulation, planners should weigh the possibility that a cornered regime chooses confrontation over concession, especially if it concludes economic pressure is merely the opening phase of a campaign for regime change.

Operation Economic Outcast may be one of Washington’s most ambitious efforts yet to sever Iran’s access to the global economy. It may weaken the regime significantly. But whether that produces diplomacy rather than a wider war will depend less on the severity of this week’s sanctions than on what Washington is prepared to do — and offer — once the deadlines it says it has communicated to foreign governments begin to expire.

Charbel A. Antoun is a Washington-based journalist and writer specializing in U.S. foreign policy, with a focus on the Middle East and North Africa.

articles.title: Attempted murder arrest after man's balcony fall in Salford
articles.summary: A man who fell from a balcony is critically injured after suffering life-threatening injuries.
articles.body:
A man has been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder after a man fell from a balcony.

Police were called to reports that the man had fallen at flats on Liverpool Street in Salford shortly after midnight on Saturday, Greater Manchester Police (GMP) said.

Emergency services attended and the man was taken to hospital with life-threatening injuries, where he remains in a critical condition, the force said.

A man in his 20s has been taken into police custody for questioning.

The incident has been referred to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) because the men had earlier contact with police, GMP said.

A blue forensic tent has been erected near to a building on the corner of Liverpool Street and Southern Street.

A local resident, who did not wish to be named, said she heard sirens overnight and saw the aftermath of the incident being live-streamed on social media.

She said: "I heard all the sirens, but I keep myself to myself so I didn't go out.

"I've seen it's all cordoned off and there's a blue forensics tent.

"It's sad, it's really sad. It's a bit close to home."

Ch Insp Lee Gridley said: "A man has been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder, and he is currently being questioned in custody.

"Our officers are working at pace to establish the full circumstances, and a scene will remain in place whilst the investigation continues.

"We understand that incidents of this nature may cause concern within the community, however we believe this is an isolated incident and that there is no wider risk to the public."

An IOPC spokesperson said: "After being notified by the Greater Manchester Police of the previous police contact with the parties involved in this incident, we sent investigators to the police post-incident procedures in Manchester in assessment mode to gather further information.

"We continue to remain in assessment mode and will assess a GMP referral in due course."
