articles.title: Cleverly quits shadow cabinet to run for London mayor
articles.summary: The capital is not set to vote on a new mayor until 2028.
articles.body:
Conservative MP Sir James Cleverly has said he is resigning from the shadow cabinet to run for London mayor.

"I am putting myself forward to be the Conservative candidate for mayor of London, because our capital needs more than an administrator," he wrote in the Times .

Sir James said he has told Tory leader Kemi Badenoch he is stepping down as shadow housing secretary, saying: "I must be free to speak about every aspect of London's future and concentrate fully on winning this race."

The capital is not set to vote on a new mayor until May 2028. Labour incumbent Sir Sadiq Khan is yet to confirm whether he will seek an unprecedented fourth term.

The Conservatives are yet to pick their candidate for the London mayoral race.

A source close to Badenoch said Cleverly "is a formidable politician and will out-campaign Khan".

Sir James, who was foreign secretary under former Prime Minister Rishi Sunak, wrote that he intended to make London a city to be proud of again.

"We must rebuild its reputation and make it, once again, the best place in the world to live, work, invest and build a business," he added.

A senior Conservative politician, Sir James has held a number of ministerial positions under three prime ministers - including roles as home secretary and education secretary.

The army reservist represented the Tories on the London Assembly before his election as MP for Braintree in 2015.

After rising through the backbenches, he unsuccessfully ran for Conservative party leader in 2024, losing out to Badenoch.

Reacting to Sir James's announcement, a source said Badenoch "really didn't want James to leave shadow cabinet", but believed "he will be a big asset in London".

Current London Mayor Sir Sadiq began his first term in 2016. Cleverly wrote that the capital has been "let down by Labour".

He accused Prime Minister Andy Burnham of treating London as a "cash cow: somewhere to tax, regulate, raid and blame".

Sir James said: "Londoners need homes they can afford to buy or rent. Entrepreneurs need to be able to start and grow businesses without being strangled by cost and regulation."

The last time Londoners voted for their mayor in May 2024, Sir Sadiq beat Conservative rival Susan Hall by more than 275,000 votes - representing a swing of 3.2% to Labour.

The mayor won nine of the 14 constituencies including two gains from the Tories, and gained 43.8% of the vote share.

Reform UK revealed its candidate for the May 2028 election in January when it announced Westminster City councillor Laila Cunningham would be running.

Reacting on social media, Reform UK leader Nigel Farage wrote the Conservatives are "done for", and said Cleverly "will not be the first Tory MP to give up any hope of winning their seat in Essex".

His announcement follows speculation in recent weeks that he would step down and launch a bid to become London's next mayor.

During his time at the London Assembly, Cleverly chaired the London Fire and Emergency Planning Authority, and also worked for Boris Johnson while he was mayor of London.

Burnham's summer tour is over - now he has to prove himself in Parliament

articles.title: Triathlete who survived alligator attack tells harrowing story of his escape: 'I got super lucky'
articles.summary: Jonathan Bruney reveals how squeezing an alligator's eye saved his arm during a Savannah River training swim near Augusta for an Ironman competition.
articles.body: A triathlete who survived an alligator attack in the Savannah River shared his story with OutKick OutDoors. Jonathan Bruney took a trip to the Georgia/ South Carolina border for what he thought would be a routine day of training for an upcoming Ironman competition. "This was a work trip for me as a coach to bring my athletes down to the river on a recon course day, is what we call it," Bruney explained. BOATER SCARED OFF ALLIGATOR, THEN USED ROPE TO STOP BLEEDING AFTER FLORIDA WOMAN LOST ARM "We all went down to Augusta, we got ready to swim, and this was just going to be a nice, easy zone-two, low-heart-rate day. Just going through each portion of the course." While he was leading the pack, Bruney felt a bump on his elbow that turned the whole day into a fight for survival. FLORIDA MAN GIVES AN INCREDIBLE INTERVIEW ABOUT HOW HE FOUGHT OFF AN ALLIGATOR WITH A FISHING POLE "I was breathing and sighting on my left side … and he was on my right. That’s when my elbow felt the brute of the force." Bruney thought the alligator, which he described to be anywhere between five and six feet, was a log. "I wasn’t even thinking gator," said Bruney. "I’m thinking, ‘Okay, big log floating in the river.’ But then I looked to my right. I’m like, ‘Okay, this is a lot worse than a log.’" Almost immediately, Bruney's fight or flight instincts kicked into overdrive. FLORIDA WILDLIFE OFFICIALS CONFIRM 13-FOOT GATOR KILLED ORLANDO WOMAN WITH 'DEATH ROLL' ON RIVER "This thing’s big enough to barrel roll and rip the arm off if I don’t get away quickly," he recalls. His next move may have ultimately saved his life, or at the very least, his arm. "I did have two moderate punches, but that didn’t do anything… [I] went up the snout and squeezed the eye." Bruney explains that he learned about the eyes being sensitive spots from watching "Shark Week" (who says you can't learn anything from TV shows). After making it to shore, Bruney wasn't just worried about his own safety, but for the safety of his fellow athletes, too. "I hope this gator doesn’t bite one of my athletes," he said. None of the swimmers had their phones on them, so a good samaritan had to dial 9-1-1. While that was taking place, a friend of Bruney's was able to stop the bleeding using a cord from his swim buoy. NEARLY 2,000 OCEAN RESCUES OCCUR AS DANGEROUS SURF SLAMS POPULAR BEACHES THIS SUMMER By the time the first responders arrived, Bruney was starting to feel dizzy and his entire arm was running cold. He credits the police officers and EMTs, who were first to arrive on the scene, with keeping him calm and treating his wounds. "The police officers, they came on scene pretty quickly. I mean, within a few minutes I heard their sirens," Bruney said. "They actually wrapped my arm up. Pretty good props to them for knowing what to do. And then the ambulance came." While the doctors cleared him to continue training for his competition, Bruney admits there was a moment of doubt. But after giving it some thought, he said there was no way he was going to let this deter him. "Being able to remove my race entry, that’s not on the books. I can’t do that." When I asked him whether he would ever go back in the water, Bruney didn't hesitate. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS "We’ll be back in there," he said, confidently.

articles.title: Suspected Florida cinnamon roll bandit wasn’t a thief — he was detained by immigration agents, bakery says
articles.summary: The case of an Uber courier accused of disappearing with thousands of dollars’ worth of cinnamon rolls in South Florida has taken a turn.
articles.body: The case of an Uber courier accused of disappearing with thousands of dollars’ worth of cinnamon rolls in South Florida has taken a turn. Julie Pierre, founder of South Florida-based viral bakery business Roll and Dough, initially believed the driver she hired to deliver 400 cinnamon rolls to a farmers’ market took off with the pastries after they never made it to their destination on Saturday. The 21-year-old took to social media on Thursday to say that she finally got the real story. “Based on the limited information available to us at the time, we believed our cinnamon rolls had been stolen,” Roll and Dough said in a statement posted on Instagram. “Uber instructed us to file a police report, so we followed their guidance.” “We did not know that the carrier, Ivan, had been detained by immigration authorities during the delivery,” the statement continued. Sunrise Police confirmed the driver was taken into custody by U.S. Border Patrol (CBP) in Hollywood while he was en route to deliver the cinnamon rolls. In a statement, a CBP spokesperson said the driver, Ivan Dario Rico Molano, was stopped at around 8:50 a.m. on Interstate 95 southbound near Sheridan Street “following a records check on a silver Kia Carnival.” “The registered owner was identified as an alien without legal immigration status. During the encounter, the driver, identified as Ivan Dario Rico Molano, a citizen of Colombia, admitted to being in the United States without legal authorization,” the spokesperson said. “Mr. Molano was arrested and transported to the Dania Beach Border Patrol Station for processing. Records indicate he entered the United States legally in May 2021, but remained beyond his authorized period of stay.” Rico Molano then contacted someone to take the vehicle, which had the storage containers with Roll and Dough’s cinnamon rolls inside, police said. Pierre said a family member of the driver found the cinnamon rolls and returned them to the police station, where Roll and Dough were able to recover them. “Based on what we now know, Ivan did not intentionally steal our cinnamon rolls. We are sincerely sorry that we described the situation that way before learning the complete circumstances,” the statement read. “We shared what we genuinely understood at the time, and now that detectives have provided us with new information, we are publicly correcting the record.” The business also said they wanted to donate a portion of their proceeds to help the driver’s family and cover any legal fees.

articles.title: In 2024, a 192,560 sq ft industrial project won approval on 22 acres beside New Jersey’s Monmouth battlefield; two years later the state paid $15 million to preserve the former strawberry farm as part of the park
articles.summary: US News: In 2024, Monmouth County officials approved a massive 192,560-square-foot industrial development on 22 acres of farmland directly adjacent to Monmouth.
articles.body: In 2024, Monmouth County officials approved a massive 192,560-square-foot industrial development on 22 acres of farmland directly adjacent to Monmouth Battlefield State Park in Manalapan, New Jersey. The site, once a strawberry farm, sat along Route 33 just steps from one of the most significant Revolutionary War battlefields in the nation. But in August 2026, the story took a dramatic turn: the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection (NJDEP) announced it had acquired the property for $15 million, preserving it as a permanent addition to the park and blocking the planned warehouses. Here's what really happened, based on official NJDEP announcements and local reporting about the acquisition and its significance:A battlefield at the edge of developmentMonmouth Battlefield State Park preserves the site of the June 28, 1778 Battle of Monmouth, a pivotal engagement in the American Revolution where George Washington’s Continental Army fought British forces to a standstill. Today, the park encompasses more than 2,700 acres of open fields, wooded trails and historic landscapes in central New Jersey.The 22-acre parcel in question lies along Route 33, directly adjacent to the park boundary. For decades it operated as a strawberry farm, part of the agricultural fabric that still surrounds the battlefield. But as development pressure increased in Monmouth County, the land became a target for industrial use, raising concerns among historians, preservationists and local residents about the impact on the battlefield’s setting and visitor experience.The 2024 approval: 192,560 square feet of industrial spaceIn July 2024, the Monmouth County Development Review Committee (DRC) reviewed plans for a large industrial project on the site. Meeting minutes and local reporting indicate that the proposal involved roughly 192,560 square feet of industrial or flex space, consistent with the warehouse and distribution facilities that have proliferated across central New Jersey in recent years.The project, filed under the name Monmouth Battlefield Flex, LLC, received county-level approvals to move forward. For proponents, the development represented jobs and tax revenue. For critics, it threatened to place a wall of industrial buildings next to a hallowed Revolutionary War landscape, altering views, increasing traffic and undermining the park’s historic character.Community pushback and a preservation campaignAlmost immediately, the approval sparked opposition. Local residents, historical societies and preservation groups argued that the battlefield’s setting was as important as the ground itself. They worried that large warehouses would visually intrude on the park, increase truck traffic on already busy Route 33 and set a precedent for further development along the battlefield’s edges.The case became a focal point in broader debates about how New Jersey balances economic development with historic and open-space preservation, especially in the lead-up to the nation’s 250th anniversary in 2026. Advocates pushed state officials to intervene, urging the use of Green Acres funding and other tools to protect the site before construction began.The state steps in: $15 million to preserve the farmIn early August 2026, the NJDEP announced that it had acquired the 22-acre property for $15 million, permanently preserving it as part of Monmouth Battlefield State Park. The purchase was made through the state’s Green Acres Program, with additional support from the federal Land and Water Conservation Fund.Acting DEP Commissioner Ed Potosnak described the acquisition as a celebration of the nation’s 250th anniversary and a commitment to protecting Revolutionary War history for future generations. The property, formerly a strawberry farm, features open fields and wooded trails that will be managed by New Jersey State Parks for future public recreation, interpretation, education and research.With this addition, Monmouth Battlefield State Park now encompasses approximately 2,764 acres, further securing the core battlefield and its surrounding landscape.What the preservation means for the battlefieldFor preservationists, the $15 million purchase is a clear statement that the setting of a historic site matters as much as the site itself. By removing the threat of nearly 200,000 square feet of industrial development, the state has: Protected views and sightlines that help visitors understand the 1778 battle; reduced the risk of increased truck traffic and noise along Route 33 next to the park; and preserved open fields and wooded areas that can be used for future trails, educational programs and archaeological research.The acquisition also aligns with new state initiatives to fund battlefield preservation, including a recently signed bill creating a 250th anniversary of the Revolutionary War license plate whose proceeds will support similar projects.From strawberry rows to historic groundThe land’s journey from strawberry farm to approved industrial site to preserved parkland illustrates the ongoing tension between development and conservation in New Jersey. For decades, it produced fruit as part of the region’s agricultural economy. In 2024, it was slated to become another link in the supply chain of warehouses and distribution centres. In 2026, it was redefined as historic ground, worthy of protection alongside the battlefield it borders.Visitors to Monmouth Battlefield State Park may not immediately notice the change on the ground—there are no new monuments or visitor facilities yet. But the absence of warehouses where they were once planned is itself a kind of monument: a choice to prioritise long-term historical and environmental value over short-term industrial gain.A model for future battlefield protectionThe Monmouth Battlefield acquisition is likely to be cited as a model for protecting other vulnerable historic sites in New Jersey and beyond. It shows how state funding programs, federal matching grants and sustained public advocacy can combine to reverse development approvals and secure irreplaceable landscapes.As the United States marks the 250th anniversary of the Revolution, the preserved 22 acres stand as both a practical buffer for the park and a symbolic reminder that the stories we choose to protect shape the landscapes we leave behind.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: At least 37 dead and hundreds evacuated after strike on Kyiv weapons depot
articles.summary: An investigation has begun into the storage of weapons for Ukraine's military near a residential area.
articles.body:
Thirty-seven people have died and almost 400 have been evacuated after a Russian drone strike hit a depot storing weapons for Ukraine's military near a residential area on the outskirts of Kyiv.

The strike caused shells, mines and drones to detonate late on Friday, triggering a blast that damaged nearby properties including a care home for the elderly and disabled, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.

He said the storage site "definitely shouldn't have been there" and that an investigation had been launched into "terrible negligence on the part of those who stored explosive right next to people".

The attack is the second to hit a munitions depot near Kyiv in recent months, prompting renewed anger.

Four children are among the 42 people injured in Friday night's explosion, according to regional head Tymur Tkachenko, with a rescue operation ongoing at the site, in the Bucha district, on Saturday.

Russia's Ministry of Defence said in a statement that its forces had targeted "an ammunition depot" in Myla, a village to the west of the Ukrainian capital, holding "components and launch boosters for FP-1/FP-2 long-range unmanned aerial vehicles".

"Everything is completely damaged," local resident Liubov Pavlenko, 45, told the BBC after inspecting her home.

"There are cracks all around the entire perimeter, and cracks around the windows. Basically, the structural integrity has been compromised."

Zelensky said the decision to store explosives in the village was "absolutely unacceptable", adding: "Criminal proceedings have been opened on charges of official negligence."

The office of Ukraine's prosecutor general earlier said it was reviewing the "legality of the placement and storage of explosive objects and materials" near residential buildings in Myla.

It said the "actions of officials who made the relevant decisions" would also be investigated.

However, Zelensky earlier stated that "there are regulations in place - ammunition cannot be stored near homes or other residential areas", adding "appropriate conclusions will certainly be drawn".

He referenced the strike on an ammunition warehouse in Vyshneve in July, which caused a secondary detonation that killed nine, injured dozens more and damaged more than 280 homes.

Friday night's explosion has raised fresh questions about why munitions were being stored so close to people's homes, especially given the regularity of Russian aerial attacks.

"The authorities, the Ministry of Defence - why was this allowed at the depots, in a place where there used to be food?" Borys Daniyluk, 61, said.

"Why were ammunition and weapons stored there, next to a populated village? There are no words, just emotions."

Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky expressed regret that a "lesson" had not been learned following the explosion in Vyshneve.

The investigation into that incident revealed serious failings on the part of a state-owned company that had not complied with regulations regarding storage of explosives near residential buildings.

Zelensky indicated that the Myla depot had been operated by Ukraine's armed forces.

"In the fifth year of the full-scale invasion, making the same mistakes over and over is criminal negligence," Koretsky said on Telegram.

"Everyone responsible, without exception, must face severe punishment so that such situations never happen again."

Meanwhile, Tkachenko said a 14-year-old was killed in a separate attack in the Boryspil district, while Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said a two-year-old had died after a Russian drone crashed in Obolonskyi.

He added that five people, including an 18-year-old girl, were injured in fresh strikes on the capital on Saturday morning. Five people have been killed across the country over the past day, according to local officials.

Zelensky reported further overnight strikes in Odesa, Dnipropetrovsk, Sumy and Zaporizhzhia, as the Ukrainian army said it had shot down 233 Russian drones.

Russia and Ukraine have been intensifying their aerial attacks in recent months, with Kyiv focusing its operations on Russian economic targets.

Ukraine has for weeks struck sites belonging to Wildberries, the country's biggest online retailer, describing the firm as a legitimate target because it supplied components to the military, which Moscow denies.

In Russia, local officials said two people had been killed and 25 injured in strikes in the Belgorod and Rostov regions in the past 24 hours.

The Moscow-appointed governor of the occupied Ukrainian region of Zaphorizhzhia said four people were injured after a Ukrainian strike hit a shopping centre.

Russian online retailer Ozon said one of its logistic centres had been hit in an overnight Ukrainian drone strike. It said it had also suspended operations at a second logistics centre and evacuate staff "due to the danger in the area".

The retailer's facilities in Krasnodar, Dagestan, Stavropol and Adygea were targeted in strikes earlier this week, resulting in several injuries and widespread damage.
